A sacristy is a room inside or directly attached to a church. It is a private, working room — not part of the main hall where worshippers sit. Think of it as a combination of a storage room and a dressing room, but exclusively for sacred religious purposes.
What It Looks Like and Where It Sits

A sacristy is typically a small-to-medium-sized room tucked away near the altar — the raised platform at the front of the church. It often has its own separate door, sometimes opening to the outside of the building, so clergy can enter without walking through the main congregation area. It is a plain, functional space — not decorated like the main church — with cabinets, drawers, a large table or counter, a sink, and hanging space for garments.

The sacristy holds everything that is needed to perform a religious service, but which should not be left out in the open church at all times. This includes:

Sacred vessels — objects used directly during worship rituals. The most important of these is the chalice, the cup used to hold wine during Holy Communion. There is also the paten (a small plate for the bread/host), and the ciborium (a covered container that holds consecrated wafers for distribution to worshippers).

Vestments — the special clothing that a priest, bishop, or minister wears during a service. These are not ordinary clothes. They are ceremonial garments, often made of fine fabric, richly decorated, and they change in color depending on the season or occasion in the church calendar. Examples include the chasuble (the outermost garment worn over everything else), the stole (a long scarf-like band worn around the neck), and the alb (a long white robe worn underneath). Vestments are carefully folded or hung in the sacristy.

Altar linens — the white cloths used to cover the altar table during services.

Books — liturgical books such as the Missal (which contains the prayers and readings for Mass) and the Lectionary (which contains the Bible passages read during services).

Candles, incense, holy water — and other items used as part of the ritual.

Keys and parish records — the sacristy sometimes serves as a secure administrative space as well.

The sacristy is a place of preparation and conclusion — it bookends every religious service.

Before the service begins, the priest (and altar servers, if any) enters the sacristy, dresses in the appropriate vestments, prepares the chalice and other sacred vessels, and says private prayers to spiritually prepare. It is a quiet, focused space — a moment of transition from the ordinary world into the sacred act of worship.

After the service ends, the priest returns to the sacristy, removes the vestments (this is called "unvesting"), carefully cleans and puts away the sacred vessels, and returns everything to its proper place. This process is done with great care because these objects are considered holy.

Parishioners who want to speak privately with a priest after a service often wait outside the sacristy door.

The person whose job it is to maintain and manage the sacristy is called a sacristan. The sacristan ensures that the correct vestments (the color and type change with the liturgical season) are laid out and ready, that the vessels are clean and polished, that candles and incense are prepared, and that everything needed for the day's service is in order. In large churches or cathedrals, this can be a full-time position.
In Which Traditions Does It Appear?

The word sacristy is most closely associated with Roman Catholic churches, but it is also used in Lutheran, Eastern Orthodox (where it may be called a diaconicon or prothesis depending on its function), and other liturgical Christian traditions.

In Anglican and Episcopal churches, the same room is more commonly called a vestry (from the word "vest," meaning to dress). The vestry serves the same purpose. So if you read about a vestry in an English context, it is essentially the same concept as a sacristy.

Some large churches have more than one sacristy — a priest's sacristy (where the clergy vest) and a working sacristy (where servers and the sacristan prepare vessels and equipment).
When You Will Encounter This Word

You are most likely to come across "sacristy" in:

  • Religious texts, liturgical guides, or descriptions of church architecture
  • Historical novels or films set in a church or monastery setting — a secret meeting, a hidden document, a dramatic conversation "in the sacristy" is a common literary device
  • Art history — paintings and sculptures sometimes depict sacristy interiors, and famous sacristies (like those in Florentine churches) are landmarks in themselves
  • Crime fiction or thrillers involving churches — the sacristy, being private and off-limits to ordinary visitors, is a natural setting for intrigue

• "The priest slipped away from the altar and returned to the sacristy to remove his vestments after the morning Mass."
  • "The sacristan had laid out the purple vestments in the sacristy, as it was the season of Advent."
  • "The old chalice had been kept in the sacristy for over three hundred years."
  • "She waited by the sacristy door, hoping to speak with the bishop before he left."

A sacristy is the private backstage room of a church where sacred clothing, vessels, and ritual objects are stored, and where clergy prepare themselves before — and tidy up after — religious services.
